newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN official sees no increase in Iraqi oil sale.
newsitem.headline: UN official sees no increase in Iraqi oil sale.

text.p: Yasushi Akashi, the U.N. humanitarian aid coordinator, said on Friday said that he did not believe there would be any increase in the income from the Iraqi oil-for-food plan during the first six months of the program.

"I think if we have $2 billion dollars every six months, that is quite sufficient for us to purchase humanitarian goods, providing we get this machinery on track and we are getting there," he told reporters.
Asked about reports that Iraq was holding talks with the United Nations on an increase in oil sales, Akashi said Iraqi Foreign Minister Mohammed Saeed al-Sahaf did not raise the issue.

Under the oil for food deal which went into effect on December 10 Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil every six months to purchase food and medicine for its people suffering under sanctions imposed in August 1990.

The program calls for a review every three months at which time the U.N. secretary-general can recommend an increase in the oil sold should there not be enough humanitarian supplies to cover basic emergencies.

But regardless of what the secretary-general may recommended, most Security Council members have said for months that the resolution authorizing the deal would not be reconsidered unless until the six months expired.
With food supplies having been delayed due to a series of technical issues, diplomats said it would be nearly impossible to judge whether the current scheme was adequate.

In Baghdad on Friday Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed said that the issue of an increase would be raised with Secretary-General Kofi Annan, presumably after he returns from Europe next week and before he files a report on March 10.

Akashi said al-Sahaf spoke to him mainly about the delays in approval various contracts for food and medicine, due in part to the Security Council's procedures and getting all the U.N. monitors on the ground.
But he said he expected all the observers to be in place by March 15 which would allow the humanitarian supplies to be distributed.
